code.title: Middleware chain built from last to first, with short-circuit

followUps:
Browsers would be told the page is not allowed, because the CORS headers are never added. UseCors must run before the endpoint so it can add Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the response and answer the preflight OPTIONS request itself.

If it comes after, routing has already sent the endpoint's response (or a 404/405 for the preflight), so the browser blocks the call even though the server worked. Rule of thumb: put UseCors after UseRouting and before UseAuthentication, so even 401 responses carry the CORS headers.

You cannot: once the first bytes of the body are sent, the status line and headers are already gone. Headers must be set before the body starts.

Use Response.OnStarting(() => { ctx.Response.Headers["X-Id"] = id; return Task.CompletedTask; });, which runs just before the first write and is the last safe moment. Check Response.HasStarted if unsure. Anything that must be known only after the body (a checksum) belongs in an HTTP trailer, or the body must be buffered first at a memory cost.

code.title: Singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes compared

followUps:
Create a new scope for each unit of work, because a BackgroundService is a singleton and has no request scope. Inject IServiceScopeFactory, then open a scope per loop iteration.

using (var scope = factory.CreateScope())
{
  var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDb>();
  await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
}

The context lives for one batch and is disposed after it. Injecting AppDb straight into the constructor would keep one context for days.

Because the root provider holds a reference to every disposable it creates so it can dispose them at shutdown, so they are never garbage collected earlier.

If a transient HttpClientHandler-like service is resolved from the root 1,000 times per second, 1,000 objects pile up per second. Resolving from a request scope fixes it, since the scope disposes them when the request ends. Create the object yourself with new or a factory when you do not need the container to own it. ValidateScopes flags some of these cases.

code.title: Minimal-API style routes with a shared filter

followUps:
On .NET 8 there is no built-in validation for minimal APIs, so you validate yourself: call Validator.TryValidateObject or FluentValidation inside the handler, or put it in an endpoint filter.

app.MapPost("/items", (Item i) => Results.Ok(i))
   .AddEndpointFilter(async (ctx, next) => {
     if (!IsValid(ctx.GetArgument<Item>(0))) return Results.ValidationProblem(errors);
     return await next(ctx); });

Return ValidationProblem so the error shape is the same as in controllers (400, dictionary of field errors). .NET 10 adds built-in support.

Group them by feature, one static class per feature that adds its routes, and use MapGroup for shared prefix, auth and filters.

var orders = app.MapGroup("/orders").RequireAuthorization();
orders.MapOrderEndpoints();   // extension in Orders/OrderEndpoints.cs

With 100 endpoints that is about 10 files of 10 routes each. Keep handlers as named methods rather than long lambdas, so they can be unit tested, and keep Program.cs to wiring only.

code.title: Route precedence: literal beats constrained beats parameter beats catch-all

followUps:
Regex is slow to run on every request and easy to get wrong, and a failed constraint produces a 404, which is a misleading answer for bad input. Constraints are meant to choose between routes, not to validate.

A pattern such as {code:regex(^[A-Z]{{3}}$)} also hides the real reason from the client: /x/ab gets 404 instead of "code must be 3 letters". Keep simple constraints like :int or :guid for disambiguation, and validate the rest in the handler returning 400 with a ProblemDetails body.

It uses the route values you pass and the current request's ambient values, then picks the endpoint whose template can be filled with them, using the same precedence and Order as matching.

For Url.Action("Get", "Orders", new { id = 5 }) or LinkGenerator.GetPathByName("GetOrder", new { id = 5 }), templates missing a required value are rejected. A named route is the most reliable, since the name picks exactly one endpoint. Extra values that no segment uses become the query string: /orders/5?page=2.

code.title: Configuration layering and options validation

followUps:
Use user secrets in development, environment variables or a secret store in production, and keep only non-secret defaults in appsettings.json because that file is committed to source control.

In development run dotnet user-secrets set "Smtp:Password" "..."; it is stored outside the repo in your profile folder. In production use environment variables (Smtp__Password) set by the host, or a vault such as Azure Key Vault added as a configuration provider. The same IConfiguration key is read in all cases, so code does not change.

It removes reflection from binding by generating the code that copies configuration values into your option classes at build time. This makes binding faster, and trimming and Native AOT safe, because reflection over types is not allowed there.

Enable it with <EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator>true</EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator> in the project file (.NET 8). Calls like config.GetSection("Smtp").Get<SmtpOptions>() are then intercepted and replaced with generated code, and the output is identical.

code.title: Where middleware and filters sit in a request

followUps:
A resource filter wraps the whole rest of the pipeline and runs before model binding, while an action filter runs after binding, immediately around the action method.

That makes resource filters the place for work that can skip binding entirely, such as a cache lookup: if the cache hits, set context.Result and the action, binding and the body parsing never run. Action filters can see and change the bound arguments (context.ActionArguments) and the returned result, so they suit auditing and argument checks.

Use [ServiceFilter(typeof(MyFilter))] or [TypeFilter], or write the filter with constructor parameters and register it in DI. A plain attribute filter cannot take constructor services, because attributes are built by the compiler with constants only.

builder.Services.AddScoped<AuditFilter>();
[ServiceFilter(typeof(AuditFilter))]
public IActionResult Save(Doc d) { ... }

ServiceFilter resolves the instance from DI (so it must be registered); TypeFilter builds it and fills the constructor from DI, without registration.

code.title: One place that maps exceptions to ProblemDetails

followUps:
Throw for unexpected failures and for cases that the caller cannot sensibly handle; return a result value for expected outcomes that happen often, such as "email already taken".

Exceptions are slow (microseconds to tens of microseconds each) and hide the control flow, so using them for normal flow in a hot path hurts: 10,000 failed logins per second would throw 10,000 exceptions. A result type like Result<T> or TypedResults.Conflict() makes the failure visible in the method signature and costs nothing. Keep exceptions for bugs and infrastructure faults.

ValidationProblemDetails is a ProblemDetails with one extra property, errors, a dictionary from field name to a list of messages. It is used for 400 responses about invalid input.

{ "status": 400, "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "errors": { "Email": ["Email is required"], "Age": ["Must be 18 or more"] } }

The plain ProblemDetails has only type, title, status, detail and instance, so it fits one general error. With [ApiController] automatic validation returns the first kind for you.

code.title: JWT signature, issuer and expiry validation with clock skew

followUps:
RS256 uses a key pair: the identity provider signs with a private key and every API verifies with the public key. HS256 uses one shared secret, so each API that can verify tokens could also forge them.

With 10 APIs and HS256, the secret must be copied to 10 places, and any one leak lets an attacker mint admin tokens. With RS256 the public keys are published at a JWKS URL and are safe to share, and keys can be rotated by adding a new key id. The cost is slightly slower signing and verification, which is rarely visible.

You cannot revoke a signed token itself, so you add a check on the server: a short token lifetime plus a deny list or a version number checked on each request.

  1. Keep access tokens to 5 to 15 minutes, so the damage window is small.
  2. Revoke the refresh token at the identity provider so no new access token is issued.
  3. For instant effect, store revoked token ids (jti) or a per-user "tokens valid after" time in a cache, and check it in OnTokenValidated.

This adds one cache lookup per request, which is the price of immediate revocation.

code.title: Resource-based authorization with ORed handlers

followUps:
Use a filtered query: put the same rule in a Where clause so the database returns only allowed rows, instead of loading everything and calling AuthorizeAsync for each row.

var docs = db.Docs.Where(d => d.OwnerId == userId
    || (isEditor && d.Department == dept));

Checking each document one by one costs N handler calls and breaks paging: page 1 of 20 may contain only 3 allowed rows. Keep the filter and the handler rule in one shared place (for example a specification), and test that they agree.

Cache it per user in memory for a short time, because membership changes rarely but is read on every request. Better still, put the department in the token claim so no lookup is needed.

Option 1: a claim in the JWT, with the cost that changes appear only when the token is renewed (up to its lifetime, say 15 minutes). Option 2: IMemoryCache keyed by user id with an absolute expiry of 1 to 5 minutes, and a distributed cache when you have several servers. Pick the expiry from how stale the business can tolerate.

code.title: Captive scoped dependency and the fix

followUps:
Convention-based middleware is created once at start-up and its constructor runs once, so it lives for the whole app like a singleton, and anything injected into the constructor lives forever.

If the constructor takes a scoped DbContext, that one context is shared by all requests, which causes the "second operation started" error. The fix is to take scoped services as parameters of InvokeAsync(HttpContext ctx, AppDb db), which are resolved per request. Alternatively implement IMiddleware, which is created per request from DI.

Give each parallel task its own context, because a DbContext is not thread-safe and allows only one operation at a time.

Create contexts with IDbContextFactory<AppDb>:

var tasks = ids.Select(async id => {
  using var db = factory.CreateDbContext();
  return await db.Orders.FindAsync(id);
});
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

Or simply await the queries one after another. Limit the degree of parallelism, since 100 contexts would also open up to 100 connections.

code.title: Structured logging with scopes

followUps:
It costs more than most middleware because it can read and write the body; with headers only the cost is small, with bodies it can be large and also a privacy risk.

Logging a 5 KB request and 20 KB response body at 1,000 requests per second means about 25 MB per second of extra log data to buffer, format and ship. Enable it only for selected paths, set RequestBodyLogLimit and ResponseBodyLogLimit, turn off body logging by default, and redact sensitive headers (they are redacted unless you whitelist them).

Sample by a rule that keeps the interesting traces: decide at the start (head sampling) with a fixed percentage, and add tail sampling in a collector to always keep errors and slow requests.

With ParentBasedSampler(new TraceIdRatioBasedSampler(0.05)) you keep 5 percent, so 10,000 requests per second become 500 traces, and the child services follow the parent decision, so traces are never half-complete. Tail sampling needs a collector that holds a trace until it ends, which costs memory but keeps all the errors. Metrics are not sampled, so alerts stay accurate.

Dependency injection still works if the types are known at build time: constructor injection of registered classes and interfaces, and the lifetimes, are all supported. What breaks is anything that needs reflection at run time.

Supported: AddSingleton<IFoo, Foo>(), factories (sp => new Foo(...)), and IOptions<T> with the binding generator. Risky: open generics such as AddSingleton(typeof(IRepo<>), typeof(Repo<>)) over value types, assembly scanning (Scrutor), and resolving by a Type built at run time, because the compiler cannot see which constructors to keep.

Usually not for the speed alone, because a warmed-up JIT can match or beat AOT at peak throughput. The gains are start-up time, memory and image size, which matter for serverless, containers that scale often, and small instances.

Example: start-up of 600 ms down to 60 ms matters when you scale to zero, but not when one instance runs for weeks. The costs are no controllers, limited reflection and a longer build. For steady traffic, measure first; ReadyToRun or tiered PGO is often enough.

code.title: Token bucket rate limiter

followUps:
A fixed window is simple but allows bursts at the edge; a token bucket allows a controlled burst and then a steady rate, so it is smoother.

Fixed window, 100 requests per minute: a client can send 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00, which is 200 in two seconds. A token bucket with capacity 100 and refill 100 per minute allows a burst of 100, but then only about 1.7 per second. Fixed window uses one counter per client; token bucket stores tokens plus a timestamp, still tiny. Sliding window is more exact, but uses more memory.

Both: put coarse, shared limits at the gateway and fine, business-aware limits in the app. The gateway protects everything before a request even reaches your servers.

A gateway limit (for example 1,000 requests per second per IP) stops floods and covers all services in one place. The app knows the user, tenant or plan, so it can give a free user 10 and a paid user 100 requests per minute. If you run several instances, app limits need a shared store such as Redis to be exact, otherwise each instance counts alone, so a limit of 100 over 4 instances can become 400.
